newsitem.title: EGYPT: Egypt gets serious about making desert bloom.
newsitem.headline: Egypt gets serious about making desert bloom.

text.p: Egypt showed it was serious about a controversial scheme to make the Western Desert bloom when it announced on Saturday the first stage in an international tender to build what it says will be the world's biggest pumping station.

The station will eventually pump 300 cubic metres (66,000 gallons) of water a second from the Aswan High Dam lake to the Toshka depression. The water will then flow north, irrigating 500,000 acres (200,000 hectares) parallel to the Nile valley.

Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak has described it as Egypt's project for the 21st century -- the only solution for the country as the Nile valley fills with people and urbanisation eats up the farmland that sustained Egyptians for millennia.

Water from the lake is already flowing into the Toshka depression from this year's exceptionally high Nile flood and this month bulldozers began work on a canal to carry the water north toward the New Valley, a group of oases in the desert.
Egyptian officials say the project follows the course of the Nile in prehistoric times and the land along the way will prove fertile as soon as the water arrives.
But one opposition party said last week the scheme was a white elephant doomed to failure when the current water levels behind the dam fall.
"To talk about creating a new delta (in the Western Desert) is absurb. It is to delude oneself and others," said al-Shaab, the newspaper of the opposition Labour Party.
It quoted irrigation experts as saying Egypt did not have enough water to waste in the desert and the water in the Toshka depression was enough to produce only one crop a year.
Some foreign economists are also dubious, saying that once the current exceptional water levels behind the dam drop, it will be massively expensive to pump it over into Toshka.
Egypt would do better to press on with land reclamation on the edges of the Nile valley and on improving the way it uses the limited water it does have, they say.
But Minister of State Youssef Boutros-Ghali told Reuters this week the cabinet was united behind the project.
"The project is a sign of the government's ability to think ahead, well into the next century, that it dares to think on this scale," he said in an interview.
"Eventually we must come out of the (Nile) valley. We can't go on using agricultural land to live on. This government wants to address problems at the root," he added.
The announcement by the Ministry of Public Works and Water Resources says the giant pumping station will have to raise the water between 21.5 and 53 metres (70 and 175 feet).

It will be powered by electricity, possibly from the hydroelectric plant at the Aswan High Dam, and the contract includes civil works, tunnels, and the supply and installation of electromechanical equipment.
The government has given no estimate of the cost but a ministry official said on Saturday it could easily exceed one billion pounds ($295 million).
The ministry invited specialised international companies to submit prequalification documents by February 18.
